core_methodology: Multiple instance learning (MIL) with max pooling and gradient flow analysis
data_sources: Generic bag-level labeled data (not financial market specific)
alpha_potential: Potential theoretical insights into gradient-based learning dynamics, but no direct trading application demonstrated

title: The Reflexivity Threshold: A Phase Transition for Multi-Agent Performative Prediction
summary: Many learning systems are performative: once deployed, their predictions change the data distribution on which future models are trained. In multi-agent settings, this feedback is routed through a network of interacting learners, so stability depends not only on the strength of performativity but also on who affects whom. We study repeated retraining in multi-agent performative prediction and identify a spectral threshold that separates stable learning from worst-case learning obstruction. Prior work often collapses cross-agent feedback into a scalar contraction constant, missing this network structure. We instead introduce the reflexivity matrix $\Gamma$, which records how strongly one agent's deployment can move another agent's best response, defined from per-agent gradient sensitivities and curvature parameters. The threshold occurs when the spectral radius of this matrix crosses one. Below the threshold, repeated retraining converges geometrically to a unique performatively stable equilibrium, with cumulative excess loss bounded uniformly in the time horizon. Above the threshold, we construct noisy supercritical instances in which every local-information learner incurs expected cumulative excess loss growing linearly for horizons up to order $1/(\rho(\Gamma)-1)$. Together, these results characterize the threshold behavior through upper and lower bounds and recover the single-agent scalar threshold from prior work as a special case.
core_methodology: The paper introduces the reflexivity matrix to analyze multi-agent performative prediction, focusing on how agents' learning affects each other through network interactions.
data_sources: Theoretical analysis without specific market data, applicable to learning systems in general.
alpha_potential: Limited direct applicability to trading; potential insights into multi-agent learning dynamics in competitive markets.

title: Charts as Epistemic Actions for Experience-Driven Agentic Data Analysis
summary: Data agents built on ReAct-style loops now execute complex analytical workflows over structured data, yet their intermediate reasoning still runs almost entirely through text. Human analysts instead move between numbers, tables, and charts, reading visual evidence to expose trends and anomalies that text summaries drop. We ask whether charts can serve as internal epistemic actions inside a data agent's reasoning loop, and how to teach an agent to use them. We first build \probe{}, a suite of 200 controlled tasks under four matched interface conditions, and find a persistent gap between what agents can read and what they choose to use. Agents score as well from self-generated charts as from numeric output, yet plotting access alone does not translate into consistent use. Task slices show that charts lead on temporal, pattern, and anomaly reasoning, while text leads on precise reading and conditional verification. We then propose \method{}, which distils two families of experience from conditioned trajectory rollouts. One family records how to select and verify analytical operations, and the other records when to invoke text, charts, or both. A trajectory judge scores outcomes and labels intermediate steps, and a validation gate admits only experience that improves held-out performance. On three held-out benchmarks with four LLM backbones, \method{} raises analytical accuracy and visual evidence quality over matched baselines, and backbones that never drew charts begin using them, all without touching model parameters.
core_methodology: Explores the use of charts as epistemic actions within data agents' reasoning loops, comparing performance across text and visual modalities
data_sources: Controlled task suite (200 tasks), no direct financial market data
alpha_potential: Limited direct application, though visual pattern detection methodology could theoretically be adapted to price chart analysis

title: Parallel AI Agent Collaboration as Graph-Structured Distributed Block Optimization
summary: Parallel AI agents can produce useful local edits yet degrade a shared solution when their edits are combined. We model this coordination problem as discrete block optimization with an exactly evaluable objective and a known dependency graph. Independent sets certify compatible edits whose verified gains, measured against the same current solution, add exactly. A coordinator constructs a safe compatible candidate and can also evaluate interacting edits to capture favorable interactions. We prove that an optimal fractional coloring yields a merger that preserves a $1/\chi_f(G)$ fraction of the total verified local improvement, where $\chi_f(G)$ is the graph's fractional chromatic number. This guarantee is tight among mergers that select a subset of the same proposals. Under conditional local-improvement guarantees and a block error-bound condition, repeated collaboration converges geometrically in the objective gap. The rate separates task structure, agent allocation, and computation cost, yielding a linear program for agent assignment and an explicit time-cost trade-off. Code-repair experiments show that verified merging resolves conflicts between individually useful edits that cause naive merging to fail. On larger conflict-free tasks, parallel agents reduce modeled completion time at higher input-token-equivalent cost. On three public road networks, fractional integration retains 922 units of verified graph-cut improvement across 90 paired runs. For route-search agents sharing exclusive access to vehicle routes, fractional scheduling reduces measured wall time by a median of 15% across twelve paired runs, with route-cost changes varying across runs.
core_methodology: Modeling multi-agent coordination as a graph-structured distributed optimization problem with guaranteed improvement bounds
data_sources: Non-financial (code repair, road networks, route optimization)
alpha_potential: Potential theoretical framework for distributed algorithmic trading agents, but no demonstrated financial applications

title: Borrowing Strength Across Stores: Transfer Learning for Choice-Based Revenue Management
summary: Large retail chains must tailor assortment and pricing decisions to local customer preferences, yet even retailers with extensive sales records often have limited data for estimating demand at the store or local market level, particularly in product categories with short selling windows. Local estimation (fitting a demand model for each store on its own) can therefore be unreliable, while pooling data across stores improves estimation precision at the cost of ignoring local demand heterogeneity. We study how retailers can balance these competing effects through transfer learning under a multinomial logit (MNL) demand model. We propose a shrinkage estimator that combines store-specific demand estimates with information pooled from other stores. Unlike the linear or quadratic settings underlying much of the existing theoretical literature on information transfer in operations, the nonlinear MNL likelihood does not admit a straightforward bias-variance decomposition. By exploiting its self-concordant-like properties, we establish finite-sample performance guarantees that characterize when information transfer improves demand estimation and how the appropriate degree of shrinkage depends on local sample size, feature dimensionality, and cross-store heterogeneity. We further derive regret bounds for downstream assortment and pricing decisions. Numerical experiments demonstrate the operational benefits of shrinkage across different data environments. An empirical study using data from several hundred stores of a European apparel retailer shows that shrinkage improves out-of-sample product prioritization and revenue capture relative to both local estimation and full pooling. Our findings demonstrate how retailers can leverage information across their store networks to improve revenue management decisions while preserving local demand differences.
core_methodology: Transfer learning with shrinkage estimator under multinomial logit (MNL) demand model
data_sources: Retail sales data from hundreds of stores of a European apparel retailer
alpha_potential: Limited direct application, though methodological insights on handling sparse data might inform market microstructure modeling

title: Lifting PCA in the Wasserstein Space
summary: Principal Component Analysis (PCA) is a fundamental tool for statistical dimension reduction, yet no canonical extension to distribution-valued data has emerged within the framework of optimal transport. While Wasserstein barycenters and Wasserstein least-squares regression provide canonical liftings of Euclidean averaging and linear regression in the Wasserstein space, an analogous principle for PCA has remained unexplored. In this paper, we introduce Lifted PCA, a canonical extension of Euclidean PCA to Wasserstein space, obtained through the framework of lifting functionals in the space of probability measures by convex extension. Starting from the classical variational formulations of PCA on the Stiefel and Grassmann manifolds, we derive two equivalent minimization problems over probability measures supported on these manifolds that correspond to Wasserstein barycenters with generalized costs. We establish an exact analogue of the equivalence between the Stiefel and Grassmann formulations of Euclidean PCA, preserving PCA's original variational structure under lifting. We further derive dual formulations and optimality conditions, and establish equivalences with multimarginal optimal transport and matching-for-teams problems. We also establish statistical consistency for empirical estimators and develop computational algorithms based on the Wasserstein barycenter formulation over the Stiefel manifold. Whereas Euclidean PCA summarizes vectors through projections onto an optimal low-dimensional linear subspace, Lifted PCA summarizes probability distributions through an optimal probability measure supported on multiple low-dimensional subspaces. Numerical experiments on distributional datasets illustrate the practical performance of the proposed methodology and its benefits for distributional data analysis.
core_methodology: Extension of PCA to Wasserstein space using convex extension of functionals in the space of probability measures, with formulations over Stiefel and Grassmann manifolds
data_sources: Probability distributions (could theoretically be applied to return distributions or other financial distributions)
alpha_potential: Potential for dimensionality reduction and pattern extraction in distributional financial data, but unclear direct trading application

title: Mastering Model Fit: Applications of the InterModel Vigorish for Interpretable Machine Learning
summary: Accuracy alone gives little information about which features or model components improve probabilistic fit, which outcomes benefit, or how fit changes during training. We introduce the InterModel Vigorish (IMV) into the Machine Intelligence space in order to express differences in fit as an expected betting advantage over a reference model. SHAP-IMV attributes gains to features through Shapley-weighted subset comparisons, Multi-IMV evaluates one-vs-rest and pairwise class discrimination, and Ablate-IMV assesses architectural components and feature groups by ablation. We evaluate these applications over ten random seeds using tabular data, images, sensor sequences, and graphs. Feature rankings vary across estimators. High one-vs-rest accuracy can accompany negligible improvement over a null, while ablation can preserve or improve fit under a fixed training budget. On six graph-classification benchmarks, we time-profile IMV over 200 training epochs, reporting seed means and ranges. The open-source imvpy library and accompanying notebooks provide code to replicate our work and to use the IMV more widely.
core_methodology: InterModel Vigorish (IMV) for evaluating machine learning model fit improvements, including SHAP-IMV for feature attribution, Multi-IMV for class discrimination, and Ablate-IMV for architectural component evaluation
data_sources: Tabular data, images, sensor sequences, and graphs
alpha_potential: Limited direct application but could be useful for model selection and feature importance analysis in trading systems

title: AI-driven Prices for Externalities and Sustainability in Production Markets
summary: Traditional competitive markets do not account for negative externalities; indirect costs that some participants impose on others, such as the cost of over-appropriating a common-pool resource (which diminishes future stock, and thus harvest, for everyone). Quantifying appropriate interventions to market prices has proven to be quite challenging. We propose a practical approach to computing market prices and allocations via a deep reinforcement learning policymaker agent, operating in an environment of other learning agents. Our policymaker allows us to tune the prices with regard to diverse objectives such as sustainability and resource wastefulness, fairness, buyers' and sellers' welfare, etc. As a highlight of our findings, our policymaker is significantly more successful in maintaining resource sustainability, compared to the market equilibrium outcome, in scarce resource environments.
core_methodology: Deep reinforcement learning policymaker agent adjusting market prices to account for externalities and sustainability
data_sources: Simulated market environments with learning agents
alpha_potential: Limited direct applicability to financial markets, more relevant policy intervention research for sustainable resource allocation

title: A Comprehensive Evaluation on Quantization Techniques for Large Language Models
summary: For large language models (LLMs), post-training quantization (PTQ) significantly reduces memory and computational overhead. Despite rapid advancements, existing papers often lack experiments on the same ground. In addition, since quantization solutions typically contain multiple components, it is important to analyze the connections among numerous existing methods to gain an in-depth understanding of this field. To bridge these gaps, we conduct an up-to-date and extensive review of the state-of-the-art methods and perform comprehensive evaluations of low-bit quantization on representative text-only LLMs on the same ground to ensure fair comparisons. To our knowledge, this fair and extensive investigation remains critically important yet significantly underexplored in the research community. To better understand the connections, we first decouple published quantization into two steps: pre-quantization transformation to reduce outliers, and quantization error mitigation to offset performance loss. Second, we extensively evaluate the impact of quantization settings, including granularity and symmetry. Third, we analyze the performance of the latest MXFP4 and NVFP4 data formats. Our experimental results first demonstrate that optimizing rotation and scaling yields the best pre-quantization transformation, while combining low-rank compensation with GPTQ occasionally outperforms using GPTQ alone. Second, we verify that finer granularity improves performance at the cost of storage and asymmetric quantization benefits activations significantly more than weights. Third, we find that the format and precision of scaling factors have a significant impact on performance; notably, rotation-based transformation is effective for INT4 but demonstrates little improvement for MXFP4 and NVFP4, inspiring further investigation in this field.
core_methodology: Evaluates post-training quantization techniques for large language models, focusing on reducing memory and computational overhead without significant performance loss.
data_sources: Text-only large language models.
alpha_potential: Potential indirect benefits for trading strategies by improving computational efficiency of language models that could be applied to text-based market data analysis.

title: Replayable Financial Agents: A Determinism-Faithfulness Assurance Harness for Tool-Using LLM Agents
summary: Replaying a financial agent requires specifying the conditions of a rerun, preserving its execution record, and deciding which parts of its behavior to compare. We introduce the Determinism-Faithfulness Assurance Harness (DFAH), a framework and practical protocol for organizing these choices. The framework distinguishes comparisons of final decisions, tool-name sets, and ordered tool names, while treating support from available evidence as a separate evaluation target. We illustrate the framework using 2,957 recorded executions in synthetic compliance-triage and data-operations tasks. One data-operations configuration repeated its recorded decision across all trials on 84% of cases, while its ordered tool-name sequence repeated on 26%. Conversely, some compliance cases retained the same tool sequence while recorded decisions changed. A case-level example shows how repeated labels accompanied different lookups and escalation calls. These observations demonstrate how the comparison level changes the description of repeated behavior. The resulting protocol connects configuration control, preservation of each attempt, comparison of records, and inspection of changed cases. DFAH provides a practical foundation for designing replay experiments and locating execution differences during the development and evaluation of financial agents.
core_methodology: Determinism-Faithfulness Assurance Harness (DFAH) for reproducible behavior of tool-using LLM agents
data_sources: Synthetic compliance-triage and data-operations tasks (non-market data)
alpha_potential: Limited for trading - primarily addresses reproducibility in agent execution rather than market signals

title: 2-Step Agent: How a Bayesian Decision Maker Learns from AI-Decision Support
summary: Prognostic predictions from ML models support human decision making in several fields, including high-stakes ones such as healthcare and the judiciary. Yet, we still lack a clear understanding of how decision makers learn from ML-based decision support (ML-DS). In this paper, we introduce a general computational framework, the 2-Step Agent, to capture how a prediction from an ML model can also be used as a source of useful information about the training data and the causal mechanism that generated it. Our framework models (i) how a prediction from an ML model affects the beliefs of a rational Bayesian agent, and (ii) how this change in beliefs affects the estimation of the causal effect, the downstream decision for a new observation, and the subsequent outcome. In addition to the framework itself, we make three contributions. First, for the multivariate linear-Gaussian setting, we derive a tractable solution for the Bayesian inference problem introduced, i.e. one in which the agent infers information about a population from an ML prediction. Second, we experimentally identify conditions under which ML-DS is beneficial compared to unassisted decision making. Third, we show that a single misaligned prior belief of the user can be sufficient for ML-DS to lead to worse downstream outcomes compared to no decision support even when the prognostic model is well-specified and the agent is perfectly rational. Hence, even under ideal conditions, ML-DS can do more harm than good.
core_methodology: Bayesian inference framework for how decision makers learn from ML model predictions
data_sources: Generic ML model predictions (not finance-specific)
alpha_potential: Potential insights into how traders might incorporate AI signals into decision-making processes, but no direct trading application demonstrated

title: A Composite Activation Function for Learning Stable Binary Representations
summary: Activation functions play a central role in neural networks by shaping internal representations. Recently, learning binary activation representations has attracted significant attention due to their advantages in computational and memory efficiency, as well as interpretability. However, training neural networks with Heaviside activations remains challenging, as their non-differentiability obstructs standard gradient-based optimization. In this paper, we propose Heavy Tailed Activation Function (HTAF), a smooth approximation to the Heaviside function that enables stable training with gradient-based optimization. We construct HTAF as a sigmoid hyperbolic tangent composite function and theoretically show that it maintains a large gradient mass around zero inputs while exhibiting slower gradient decay in the tail regions. We show that Spiking Neural Networks, Binary Neural Networks and Deep Heaviside neural Networks can be trained stably using HTAF with gradient-based optimization. Finally, we introduce Implicit Concept Bottleneck Models (ICBMs), an interpretable image model that leverages HTAF to induce discrete feature representations. Extensive experiments across various architectures and image datasets demonstrate that ICBM enables stable discretization while achieving prediction performance comparable to or better than standard models.
core_methodology: Proposes Heavy Tailed Activation Function (HTAF) as a smooth approximation to Heaviside function for stable binary representation learning
data_sources: Primarily validated on image datasets (no financial data tested)
alpha_potential: Potential benefits in computational efficiency for neural networks, but no direct financial application demonstrated

title: A Novel Schur Decomposition-Based Weight Projection Method for Stable State-Space Neural-Network Architectures
summary: Building black-box models for dynamical systems from data is a challenging problem in machine learning, especially when asymptotic stability guarantees are required. In this paper, we introduce a novel stability-ensuring and backpropagation-compatible projection scheme based on the Schur decomposition for the state matrix of linear discrete-time state-space layers, as well as an alternative pre-factorized formulation of the methodology. The proposed methods dynamically project the quasi-triangular factor of the state matrix's real Schur decomposition onto its nearest stable peer, ensuring stable dynamics with minimal overparameterization. Experiments on synthetic linear systems demonstrate that, despite a marginal increase in computational complexity, the method achieves accuracy and convergence rates comparable to those of state-of-the-art stable-system identification techniques. Furthermore, the lower weight count facilitates convergence during training without sacrificing accuracy in stacked neural-network architectures with static nonlinearities targeting real-world datasets. These results suggest that the Schur-based projection provides a numerically robust framework for identifying complex dynamics on par with the state of the art while satisfying strict asymptotic-stability requirements.
core_methodology: Schur decomposition-based weight projection for stable state-space neural networks
data_sources: Synthetic linear systems and real-world datasets for system identification
alpha_potential: Potential for modeling stable market dynamics in time-series prediction, but no direct trading application demonstrated

title: Observation Assimilation Transformer: Probabilistic Weather Analysis from Sparse Station Observations
summary: We present the Observation Assimilation Transformer (OAT), a geometry-aware neural process that corrects and refines a prior numerical weather prediction (NWP) field into a high-resolution posterior field by assimilating sparse observations. OAT is an encoder-decoder transformer that considers a set of observed locations and their NWP prior to condition predictions at a set of arbitrary unobserved query locations. Its sparse attention mechanism makes it scalable to thousands of station observations and depends on relative positions between locations, never on the absolute coordinates. The model allows for partially missing observations, predictions at arbitrary continuous locations without grid projection, and outputs are parametric distributions. A station-randomized training algorithm is developed with continuous ranked probability score (CRPS) loss. We test OAT on two datasets - one at regional scale with hundreds of stations, and one at continental scale with thousands of stations. On these datasets OAT outperforms several baselines and shows well calibrated predictions. In an illustrative case study, OAT's downscaling capabilities are demonstrated by downscaling ERA5 (~31km) to COSMO (1km), where OAT achieves lower mean absolute error (MAE) and CRPS for temperature and precipitation on test stations compared to COSMO.
core_methodology: Geometry-aware transformer for assimilating sparse observations into numerical weather predictions
data_sources: Weather station observations and numerical weather prediction models
alpha_potential: Potential extension to assimilate alternative data sources for commodity trading

title: Planning under Noise with Neural Operators
summary: Planning under uncertain control execution noise requires reliable feedback policies across diverse environments. We introduce Planning Under Noise (PUN), a neural operator that learns noise-aware value fields for planning in unseen geometries. Building on an established screened-Poisson formulation of stochastic optimal control, we address two challenges: specifying boundary conditions that support navigation across varying geometries and efficiently computing fields with reliable gradients. Zero-Dirichlet obstacle boundaries terminate sampled paths at walls, weakening the goal signal along long routes and making it harder to estimate reliably. We instead impose reflecting Neumann conditions on obstacles and a Dirichlet condition at the goal, allowing sampled paths to continue exploring free space until they reach the target. To solve the resulting PDE without a configuration-space mesh, we extend a Monte Carlo (MC) solver, Walk on Stars (WoSt), to higher dimensions. However, local MC fluctuations can reverse estimated gradient directions and cause planning failures, making direct planning require costly sampling. PUN amortizes this computation by learning geometry-to-field mappings from noisy, partially converged Monte Carlo labels, avoiding expensive convergence for every training example. At inference, test-time scaling uses bounded local search guided by the predicted global field. We evaluate PUN on planning tasks across dimensions. Across four noise levels, PUN matches or outperforms all compared planners, achieving 95-100% success on the 4D replanning benchmark while maintaining the lowest runtime. At the highest tested noise level in 4D, PUN achieves 10.7-60.6% relative gains in success rate over other methods while running 3.29-32.15 times faster.
core_methodology: Neural operator learning noise-aware value fields for planning in dynamic environments using Monte Carlo methods
data_sources: None specified (focuses on geometric planning tasks)
alpha_potential: Potential theoretical foundation for execution algorithms in noisy environments, but not directly applicable to market data

title: Gate Initialisation versus Recurrent Dropout and Zoneout in Learning Long Dependencies: A Controlled Study of LSTM and GRU Networks on Synthetic Tasks
summary: Dropout and zoneout are routinely added to long short-term memory (LSTM) and gated recurrent unit (GRU) networks, but, to our knowledge, their placements have not been crossed with gate initialisation in a factorial design, and it is not known whether early gradient propagation tells which runs will learn long dependencies. We trained one-layer LSTMs and GRUs on the adding problem and on delayed recall in a factorial grid of 720 runs, crossing conventional and chrono gate initialisation with up to six recurrent regulariser placements at one rate each, with pre-specified follow-ups, and recorded how sensitive the final hidden state was to the input at every lag. Because both tasks supply fresh or exhaustive training data, the study measures the regularisers' effects on optimisation and does not assess generalisation from a finite training set. At lengths chosen to make conventional initialisation difficult, all 360 chrono-initialised runs reached the validation criterion within 5000 updates, as did 119 of 120 unregularised runs with a horizon about four times too short or too long, whereas conventionally initialised networks learned slowly or did not reach the criterion within the budget at the longer lengths. Under conventional initialisation, dropout generally delayed learning and zoneout helped only in some conditions. The early input sensitivity added little to predicting which conditions learn once the early validation loss was modelled per task, architecture and initialisation. Within conditions, a flatter early decay went with the seeds that learned, but in a pre-specified test the association was modest (concordance 0.61), condition-dependent and not robust to resampling seeds. The results support chrono initialisation, even with a rough horizon, on such tasks.
core_methodology: Controlled study comparing different initialization techniques (chrono and conventional) and regularization methods (dropout, zoneout) in LSTM and GRU networks on synthetic tasks.
data_sources: Synthetic data (adding problem and delayed recall tasks).
alpha_potential: Limited direct applicability; insights may help improve RNN architectures for time series prediction, but no direct trading signal or financial application tested.

title: Private Online Prediction from Experts with Small Losses
summary: We consider online prediction from experts, a fundamental problem in machine learning, under differential privacy constraints. Existing private algorithms achieve near-optimal regret $\tilde{O}(\sqrt{T})$, where $T$ is the time horizon. However, this bound becomes suboptimal when $L^\star$, the cumulative loss of the best expert, is significantly less than $T$. In this work, we present the first differentially private algorithm with regret $\tilde{O}(\sqrt{L^\star})$, offering a substantial improvement in the low-loss regime. Our regret bound matches the non-private lower bound up to poly-logarithmic factors for constant privacy parameters, demonstrating that privacy incurs only a small cost in this setting. Our result assumes that the input sequence is oblivious, i.e., it is fixed in advance and independent of the algorithm's outputs. We also prove that an $\tilde{\Omega}(\sqrt{T})$ regret is inevitable for adaptively generated inputs, even when $L^\star = 0$.
core_methodology: Differentially private online prediction from experts
data_sources: Generic input sequence (not market-specific)
alpha_potential: Limited; theoretical improvement in low-loss regime but lacks financial context

title: Preventing Model Extraction in Contextual Linear Optimization
summary: Consider a contextual linear optimization problem, where a predict-then-optimize (PTO) system returns optimal decisions without revealing the cost vectors used in its downstream linear program. Our focus is on how to prevent attackers, who can submit context queries, from extracting the underlying prediction model. Although the cost-to-decision map is many-to-one, observations across contexts can reveal the underlying prediction model. For linear models, we provide sufficient conditions where the attacker can learn the model up to positive scaling by only observing the decision. These conditions motivate an adaptive attack that alternates inverse optimization with boundary sampling, i.e., using context queries leading to decision boundaries of the current attacker model. To prevent extraction, we propose a mechanism that perturbs decisions only when the predicted cost vector is near a decision boundary. We establish a regret bound in terms of the perturbation radius. For the attackers that fit the defended responses as optimal decisions under the evaluation distribution, we also prove a lower bound on expected extraction error. Experiments on synthetic instances and real data quantify the security-performance trade-off of the defense mechanism and illustrate that our defense can increase the extraction error.
core_methodology: Preventing model extraction via decision boundary-aware perturbation in contextual linear optimization
data_sources: Synthetic and real data (unspecified domain)
alpha_potential: Limited direct trading application - focuses on security rather than alpha generation

title: First Passage Attention
summary: Augmenting softmax attention with forget gates typically relies on summing decay contributions along the key--query path. Because such accumulation is monotonic, these mechanisms cannot selectively erase intermediate context while preserving older, structurally relevant tokens. We propose First Passage Attention (FPA), which shifts from path summation to path extrema by lowering a key's logit proportionally to the deepest dip of a learned scalar field below that key's level over the intervening span. FPA encompasses the Forgetting Transformer (FoX) as a special case, and when the field and levels follow a shared learned walk, the alive keys with unpenalised logits naturally form a stack. We show that a constant-dimension FPA head realises any subset of keys left alive by subsequent dips, whereas softmax heads with positional biases or token-level forget gates require a head dimension linear in the number of keys. In synthetic experiments, one-layer FPA heads converge to these target sets while comparable softmax and FoX baselines fail on every seed. Scaling to a 110M-parameter language model, FPA matches FoX in perplexity and uniquely achieves perfect passkey retrieval at $8\times$ the training length, even with its key--value cache compressed to about $25\%$.
core_methodology: Proposes First Passage Attention (FPA), a novel attention mechanism in transformers that uses path extrema instead of path summation for better context selection
data_sources: Primarily tested on synthetic data and language modeling (110M-parameter LLM)
alpha_potential: Potential but unproven applications in market sentiment analysis or news interpretation via improved context handling in financial NLP tasks

title: A Jump-Modified Wasserstein Gradient Flow for Maximum Mean Discrepancy with Energy Kernels
summary: We study a jump-modified Wasserstein gradient flow of the squared maximum mean discrepancy generated by the energy kernels $K(z)=-|z|^q$, $0<q<2$, in every dimension $d\ge2$ as well as the one-dimensional range $1\le q<2$. Under subcritical density and finite-moment assumptions, we prove global well-posedness. The added jumps transfer mass toward smaller values of the first variation and dissipate the same MMD energy as the transport term. Under our hypotheses on the target and jump rates, every Borel probability measure with finite MMD energy and zero jump dissipation is equal to the target. Combining this rigidity with compactness and a second-moment identity yields convergence to the target from finite-second-moment data, without additional uniform-in-time density or moment assumptions. We also construct a global collision-free particle process whose energy is nonincreasing along each path. A quantitative mean-field estimate applies to general initial empirical approximations, including deterministic configurations; propagation of chaos for exchangeable data and long-time target approximation follow as consequences.
core_methodology: Jump-modified Wasserstein gradient flow for optimizing maximum mean discrepancy with energy kernels
data_sources: Theoretical mathematical constructs (probability measures, density functions)
alpha_potential: Limited direct applicability; potential theoretical basis for distributional approaches in finance, but no clear trading signal extraction

title: Group Distributionally Robust Optimization over Decentralized Networks
summary: We study group distributionally robust optimization (GDRO) over decentralized networks, where workers collaborate to learn robust models by minimizing the maximum local risk. Existing methods optimize only dual-regularized surrogates and establish guarantees for a globally averaged model that is not available to workers. In this paper, we directly optimize the original GDRO objective and establish guarantees for local models in semi-decentralized (SemiDec) and fully decentralized (Dec) settings. A key difficulty is that applying the primal-dual decomposition from centralized GDRO yields worker-dependent losses whose evaluation requires unavailable cross-worker information. To address this challenge, we develop a novel error decomposition that recasts decentralized GDRO as (i) a decentralized online convex optimization (D-OCO) problem and a prediction-with-expert-advice problem in SemiDec, and as (ii) two coupled D-OCO problems in Dec, with discrepancy terms capturing inconsistencies among local decisions. By isolating consensus errors in analysis, we develop modular frameworks that support different consensus routines. We then establish the \emph{first} per-worker convergence guarantees for optimizing the original GDRO objective over decentralized networks. Instantiations with accelerated gossip and Choco-gossip achieve an $O(\sqrt{(\log m)/T})$ convergence rate over $T$ update rounds, while experiments demonstrate improved worst-worker performance over baselines.

title: DFAH-Bench: What Agreement Leaves Unmeasured in Financial Agents
summary: When a financial agent repeats its decision, how much does that tell us about the actions behind it? DFAH-Bench examines this question through replay experiments, a controlled test of omitted tool calls, and banking tasks with authorization checks. Across 570 eligible prospective replay episodes, decisions agreed at rates of 94-95%, while tool paths, including inputs and results, agreed at 45-52%; one condition fell one group short of the planned minimum. In a separate 48-execution diagnostic, deleting the same calls from repeated records left agreement perfect. In banking probes, repeated authorization decisions sometimes conflicted with constructed rule labels. The $\tau$-Knowledge banking study scheduled 1,080 episodes, with 1,033 known outcomes. Structural checks alone completed more primary tasks than either model-based gate-and-recovery bundle. Input limits and recovery behavior materially shape these results. The typed-choice bundle had lower mean episode cost than the generative bundle on complete task pairs, but fewer successes across the primary schedule under every assignment of unknown outcomes. Missing outcomes prevented the planned confirmatory tests, so the banking comparisons are descriptive. Together, the findings show that agreement alone cannot establish reliability: it can conceal changes in execution, systematic omissions, and unsupported decisions. Evaluation therefore needs to connect what the agent did, the evidence and rules governing its action, and whether it completed the task.

title: Self-organizing reinforcement learning: a learner-free swarm approaches the explore-exploit optimum
summary: The explore/exploit trade-off is the core problem of reinforcement learning (RL). We show that a minimal foraging swarm approaches its optimum - the ideal-free / Nash allocation of a multi-agent resource-sharing game (an equilibrium, not a return maximum) - with no learner and no reward signal. Agents explore by heavy-tailed (Levy) flights, recruit neighbours to a discovery through a threshold cascade on their proximity network, and disperse as a patch crowds; this cascade cycle balances exploration and exploitation and drives foragers toward the ideal free distribution. The swarm attains the shape of this optimum (committed foragers track richness with slope 0.94) but not its exact equilibrium - it stays measurably exploitable - reaching it dynamically (~150 steps) through the coupling of recruitment to movement: remove the coupling and matching collapses (0.94 -> 0.08). The RL sits at the level of the problem and the allocation reached, not the micro-rule: no step evaluates payoff (reward-free by construction, though the crowd signal is informationally tied to payoff), and the swarm reaches the allocation without learning it (quality plateaus and re-settles after resources move, no cumulative gain). Against a trained baseline the comparison is two-sided: in an easier, disembodied game a learner is more precise, while in the same embodied environment the reward-free swarm reaches ~65% of a validated oracle ceiling at zero training and leads until trained PPO and centralised-critic (CTDE) learners overtake it (~74-75%, 16 seeds, all above the swarm mean) after ~4,000 of 15,000 training steps - its advantage is in budget, not asymptote. In this one setting we read it not as beating RL but as a strong zero-shot, reward-free operating point: a demonstration that the self-organizing physics of a minimal swarm can carry a collective close to the optimum RL seeks, with none of RL's machinery.
